rationale: A wins because it keeps three clean stories inside the facts. "Sweetgreen says automation lifts margins — its bottom line still says otherwise" is a real finance-desk test; B spends its credibility on "The $15 salad is now assembled by robot" and "premium, customizable, ingredient-forward," neither of which appears in the update. Two good B angles do not rescue one invented premise. That's how you turn a usable announcement into homework for legal.
gaps_in_A: "concrete, citable case of reduced staff hours tied to automated assembly" slightly overstates the supplied fact; the update says only that "some worry about reduced staff hours," not that cuts have happened.
"Sweetgreen makes robot-assembled bowls the default" pushes "most new stores" into "default"; defensible, but it needs the actual pipeline share before that word is safe.
The financial angle admits "there's no stated earnings date," so the why-now is a thin company-disclosure window, not a strong external peg.
gaps_in_B: "The $15 salad is now assembled by robot" invents a price point. It may feel true to anyone who has bought lunch, but it is not in the update.
"premium, customizable, ingredient-forward" and "the tier where automation couldn't go" invent a category premise the facts do not support.
"McDonald's, Chipotle's Autocado, etc." drags in competitor automation facts not supplied. A correctly killed that exact move as hallucinated.
"ongoing fights around restaurant-worker protections and minimum wage" is a generic backdrop, not a real supplied why-now peg.
